title: How to plan lessons faster with little planning time on Mac: a teacher's routine
metaTitle: Plan Lessons Faster With Little Planning Time on Mac
description: Plan lessons faster with little planning time using a repeatable routine in Pages, Google Docs, Notes and Gmail on your Mac. Free fixes first.
targetKeyword: plan lessons faster with little planning time
intro: You can plan lessons faster with little planning time by reusing one lesson skeleton, writing the exit ticket first, and sending every idea to one place. The gain comes from deciding less each time. Typing faster helps much less than most teachers expect.
tldr: Reuse one lesson skeleton for every class, so each short window starts with structure instead of a blank page.
Write the exit ticket first, then fill the middle of the lesson. A short window is enough for one decision.
Dictate ideas with fn between classes and park them in a Notes folder. Clear that folder in one sitting.
Lazur can point at things on screen, answer questions out loud and draft text. It does not click for you or plan the lesson.

blocks.text: Short prep periods are not a rare problem. In a 2024 Pew Research Center survey, 84% of U.S. public K-12 teachers said they do not have enough time in their regular work hours. That time covers grading, lesson planning, paperwork and email. If your planning window is a few minutes between classes, you are in a large group. This page covers what the gap costs, why it happens, and what you can change on your Mac this week.
What a short prep period really costs you

Planning time is small on paper too. The National Council on Teacher Quality (NCTQ) reports that public school teachers get about 53 minutes of planning time a day. That is just under 4.5 hours a week. NCTQ cites NCES as the most recent national figure. Its contract sample averages 51 minutes a day, and about one-third of sampled districts give roughly four hours a week.

Some teachers get nothing at all. NCTQ cites a 2024 Arkansas teacher survey in which nearly 40% of teachers reported no planning time. A separate small survey, the Planning Period Project, found 25% of respondents got zero minutes of planning on the day they answered. That survey had 300 responses from 36 states. Treat it as a signal, not a national count.

The workload has a second side. OECD data cited by NCTQ shows U.S. teachers work 46.2 hours a week, against 38.8 across OECD countries. Their preparation and lesson planning takes 5.1 hours a week, compared with 5.4 hours for the OECD average. So the problem is less about total effort. It is more about where the hours go.
Why short planning windows keep shrinking

Pew asked the same teachers why time runs short. Most say simply having too much work is a major reason. Pew's chart describes this as about 8 in 10. Other major reasons are non-teaching duties such as hallway or lunch duty, cited by 24%, and covering another teacher's class, cited by 16%.

The Planning Period Project asked teachers what took their planning time. Planned and unplanned meetings took 35% of the lost time. Direct contact with students or parents took 29%. Administrative tasks took 18%. Other tasks took 13%, and covering other teachers' classes took 5%.

items: Meetings, planned and unplanned: 35%
Direct contact with students or parents: 29%
Administrative tasks: 18%
Other tasks: 13%
Covering other teachers' classes: 5%

blocks.text: That survey was small and not representative, so use these shares to spot patterns, not to set policy. The pattern still lines up with Pew. Meetings, contact, duties and coverage crowd out planning. Your own calendar will show which one is yours.
A worked example: one short window before lunch

Say you have one short window before lunch, and a meeting after it. Tomorrow you teach equivalent fractions, and you have no skeleton for it yet. The slow way is to open a blank document, search for ideas, and stop when the window ends. The faster way has a few short moves, and each one needs little thinking.

items: Open last month's lesson skeleton in Google Docs or Pages, not a blank page.
Type the exit ticket question first. One question is enough to set the goal.
Hold fn and dictate the warm-up idea into the document. Read it back once.
Drop every other idea into a Notes folder for the next free period.

blocks.text: The window only has to hold a few decisions. The lesson itself can wait for the next free period. That split is the whole method.
Build one lesson skeleton you reuse

A skeleton is a template with blanks. It holds the same sections every time, and you fill in only the content. Keep it short. A long template takes longer to fill than a blank page, and that defeats the point.

In Google Docs, choose File > New > From template gallery, or build one document and save a copy for each unit. In Pages, choose File > New to open the template chooser. Pick a simple template, remove what you do not use, and save it once as your base. If your lesson uses slides, Keynote can hold the same skeleton. Google Docs runs in your browser, so check that editing works on your school's setup before you rely on it. See /for/teachers/google-docs for more.
A basic skeleton needs only a few headings. Keep them in the order you teach them, and reuse the same order every day.

items: Learning goal, written in student language
Warm-up, one question that takes a few minutes
Mini lesson, the one idea you teach
Practice, the task students complete
Exit ticket, the check for understanding

blocks.text: Plan backward from the exit ticket

Most short windows fail because the goal is too big. Start from the exit ticket instead. Ask what one question would show that students got the idea. If you cannot write that question quickly, the goal is too large. Split it, then plan the smaller piece.

blocks.title: Test your goal
blocks.text: Write the goal, then the exit ticket. If the exit ticket needs a second lesson to answer, cut the goal in half and try again.

Keep a folder of exit tickets from past units in Pages or Google Docs. When a unit comes back, pull the question, adjust the wording, and move on. A question you already wrote costs much less time than a new one.
Capture ideas between classes in Notes

Ideas show up in the hallway, in the car, and in the middle of a class. Write them down before they fade. Apple Notes works well for this. Press ⌘N for a new note, add a folder from the sidebar, and keep one folder for each unit.

Apple's Notes guide describes live audio recording with searchable transcripts, Markup drawing tools, and management of PDFs and scanned documents. Use audio when your hands are full. Do not record student names or work samples unless your school allows it.
Dictate with fn when your hands are busy

Hold fn in any app and speak. Lazur dictates clean, formatted text at your cursor. Snippets, a personal dictionary and clipboard slots help with phrases you repeat, such as learning goals and standard codes. Dictation is not capped on either paid plan.

blocks.title: Read before you send
blocks.text: Dictation makes mistakes with names, numbers and technical terms. Read the text once before it goes to a student, a parent or a colleague.
Split planning with a colleague in Reminders

Shared work helps most when windows are short. In Reminders, select a list in the sidebar and click Share to invite a colleague. Invitees must accept before they can view and edit. You can turn off their ability to add other people. Stopping the share removes the list from everyone's devices.

Sharing needs an updated iCloud Reminders account. Other account types lose some features. Use the list for handoffs, such as who drafts Monday's exit ticket and who checks Friday's quiz. Keep the lesson files in Pages or Google Docs, and paste the link into the reminder.
Use Gmail templates for parent email

Parent emails eat short windows. Gmail templates let you write a reply once and reuse it. Choose Settings > See all settings > Advanced, turn on Templates, and save. Then open a new message and insert the saved template from the More options menu. For a full routine, read /for/teachers/problems/reply-parent-emails-quickly-teachers.
Use AI for first drafts, within school rules

AI helps most with first drafts. Among teachers who use AI at least monthly, the most common use is lesson preparation, at 37%. Worksheet creation comes next at 33%. Adapting materials for students is at 28%, and administrative work is also at 28%.

These time savings are self-reported. In a Walton Family Foundation survey with Gallup, weekly AI users said they save an average of 5.9 hours each week. Monthly users reported 2.9 hours. Only 32% of teachers use AI at least weekly, and 40% do not use it.

Policy matters too. The same survey found only 19% of teachers say their school has an AI policy. Schools with a policy save about 2.3 hours a week per teacher, against 1.7 hours without one. Check your school's rules before you put student names, grades or work into any AI tool.

blocks.title: A safe default
blocks.text: Let AI draft the skeleton and sample questions. Then rewrite the questions yourself and check every fact before class.
Where Lazur fits in a short prep period

Lazur is a voice assistant that lives in the notch on your Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and it draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

That helps in short windows when you do a task rarely. You might not remember where Google Docs keeps templates, or where the Share button sits in Reminders. Ask. Lazur points, and you make every click yourself.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. It also does not plan your lessons. It helps you find the next step and draft text that you then check.
What to ask Lazur during a prep period

items: Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask what an error in Pages means.
Ask where the Share button is in Reminders.
Ask Lazur to walk you through making a template in Google Docs.
Ask Lazur to set a timer for the mini lesson.
Ask Lazur to draft a short exit ticket on a topic you name, then edit it.

blocks.text: Lazur can also run research in the background. That work runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary and a report. Use it to find a reading or practice set on a topic you teach. Then open the sources yourself, because a summary can miss context.
Mistakes that eat the window

items: Opening the whole unit plan before you know the goal.
Starting in a blank document every time.
Typing notes you could dictate in a few seconds.
Pasting student names or grades into any AI tool without checking school rules.
Accepting the first AI draft without reading it.
Never telling an administrator which meetings take your planning time.

blocks.text: The last mistake is the easiest to fix, and the most often skipped. Bring one week of your calendar to your administrator. Mark the meetings and duties that landed in planning time. The Planning Period Project author says easily more than half of lost time involves activities an administrator could control or limit.
When you have almost no planning time

Some windows are too short to plan anything. In that case, do one thing. Open the skeleton, write the learning goal, and stop. A half-finished skeleton is still ahead of a blank page the next morning.

If planning time goes to coverage, say so in writing. Covering other teachers' classes took 5% of lost planning time in the Planning Period Project. Pew lists it as a major reason for 16% of teachers. The share is small, but it repeats every week, so keep a simple log.
A realistic week with short windows

rows: Fill the learning goal and exit ticket for tomorrow
Dictate the warm-up idea and any materials to find
Build the middle of the lesson from the skeleton
Clear the Notes folder and send parent replies from templates
Split the next week's planning with a colleague
blocks.caption: A routine built around short windows, not one long block.

blocks.text: Start with the skeleton. It pays back in every window after it. If you want Lazur on your Mac, the download is at /download, and plans are at /pricing. faq.question: How much planning time do teachers usually get?
faq.answer: NCTQ reports public school teachers get about 53 minutes of planning time a day, or just under 4.5 hours a week, citing NCES. Its contract sample averages 51 minutes a day. Your own contract sets your real number, so check it before you plan around it.

faq.question: Can I plan a full lesson in a short window?
faq.answer: Usually no. Plan one decision in the window, such as the exit ticket or the warm-up. Leave the middle for a longer free period. A reusable skeleton makes the next short window faster.

faq.question: Is it okay to use AI for lesson plans?
faq.answer: It depends on your school. Only 19% of teachers in a Walton Family Foundation survey say their school has an AI policy. Check the rules first, keep student names out of prompts, and read every output before you use it.

faq.question: Does Lazur keep what I say or show it?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Follow your school's rules on student data either way.

faq.question: Can Lazur fill in my lesson plan for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur can draft text when you ask, and it can guide you through steps. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. You still write, check and decide what reaches students.

faq.question: Does Lazur run on Windows?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is for macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available yet.

faq.question: Is there a free trial?
faq.answer: Yes. Lazur has a free trial with no credit card. It starts the first time you open the app. Plan details are on /pricing.

faq.question: Can I share Apple Notes with a colleague?
faq.answer: Apple's Notes guide lists sharing and collaboration. For handoffs, a shared Reminders list is simpler to explain. Use Notes for ideas you keep to yourself or for a folder you share on purpose.

costs.title: Longer weeks with less prep
costs.text: U.S. teachers work 46.2 hours a week on average, against 38.8 across OECD countries, according to OECD data cited by NCTQ. Preparation and lesson planning takes 5.1 hours, against 5.4 for the OECD average. When a window disappears, the planning does not. It usually moves to your evening or weekend.

costs.title: Rushed plans with gaps
costs.text: The research I could open does not measure how short windows change lesson quality, so this page will not claim a number. You can feel the cost, though. A plan written in spare minutes often has gaps you only notice in front of the class.

costs.title: Zero planning on some days
costs.text: For some teachers the cost is total. In one small survey, 25% of respondents got zero minutes of planning on the day they answered. In an Arkansas survey cited by NCTQ, nearly 40% of teachers reported no planning time. These teachers need a fix that works with no window at all.

causes.title: Too much work in the regular day
causes.text: Pew asked U.S. public K-12 teachers why they lack planning time. Most say having too much work is a major reason, which Pew's chart describes as about 8 in 10. Grading, paperwork and email share the same hours. Planning has no bell, so it is easy to push aside.

causes.title: Meetings and student or parent contact
causes.text: In the Planning Period Project, planned and unplanned meetings took 35% of lost planning time. Direct contact with students or parents took 29%. The survey was small and not representative, but the pattern is easy to check against your own week.

causes.title: Coverage and non-teaching duties
causes.text: Pew reports that non-teaching duties such as hallway or lunch duty are a major reason for 24% of teachers. Covering another teacher's class is a major reason for 16%. Duties take the middle of a free period, and coverage can take the whole thing.

causes.title: Schedules that do not protect planning
causes.text: NCTQ says the average planning time in its contract sample is 51 minutes a day. About one-third of sampled districts give roughly four hours a week. Teachers in the same building can get very different windows. Your contract and bell schedule decide the size of your window.

fixes.title: Build one skeleton and reuse it
fixes.text: Make one template in Pages or Google Docs with the same headings for every lesson. Fill the content, not the structure. Save a copy for each unit so the base stays clean. This is the single change that saves the most time in short windows.

fixes.title: Write the exit ticket first
fixes.text: Start each lesson from the question that shows whether students got it. Write that question before the warm-up or the activities. If the question is hard to write, the goal is too big, so shrink the goal.

fixes.title: Park ideas in one Notes folder
fixes.text: Keep a single Notes folder for each unit. Press ⌘N whenever an idea shows up, even in the middle of class. Clear the folder in one sitting during your free period, and move the good ideas into the skeleton.

fixes.title: Dictate between classes with fn
fixes.text: Hold fn and speak instead of typing a half-formed plan. The text lands at your cursor, cleaned up. Read it once before you rely on it, since names and terms are where dictation most often fails.

fixes.title: Split the week with a colleague
fixes.text: Share a Reminders list with a colleague who teaches the same subject. Each of you drafts different days, then hands the list over. Invitees must accept the share first, so set it up together in one short meeting.

fixes.title: Save parent replies as Gmail templates
fixes.text: Write the replies you send most often once, then save them as templates. Edit the student name and details before each send. Keep grades out of templates unless your school allows it.

fixes.title: Take the meeting problem to your administrator
fixes.text: Bring a week of calendar entries and show which meetings and duties landed in planning time. The Planning Period Project author says easily more than half of lost time involves activities an administrator could control. Ask for one protected window, not a full rebuild.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Fill the goal and exit ticket
plan.text: Open tomorrow's skeleton in Pages or Google Docs. Write the learning goal in student language, then the exit ticket question. Leave the middle blank if the plan is not clear yet.

plan.label: Between classes
plan.title: Dictate, do not type
plan.text: Hold fn and speak any idea you want to keep. Keep sentences short. Read the result before you move on, so errors do not travel into the lesson.

plan.label: Free period
plan.title: Build the middle
plan.text: Fill the warm-up, mini lesson and practice from the skeleton. Use last unit's exit tickets as examples. Stop when the bell rings, even if the middle is rough.

plan.label: After school
plan.title: Clear the Notes folder
plan.text: Move ideas from the unit folder into the right skeleton. Delete ideas you no longer need. Send parent replies from saved Gmail templates.

plan.label: Weekly
plan.title: Split the next week
plan.text: Share a Reminders list with a colleague. Divide the days, then hand off the drafts. Review what worked and update the skeleton.
